sentences.text: Tribodus stands out among hybodonts, a group of extinct sharks, because fossils are often found as articulated and nearly complete skeletons.
The type species, Tribodus limae — the specimen the species is based on — reached a total length of about 1 meter.
Its teeth were specialized for durophagy, meaning it ate hard-shelled organisms.
Evidence of shrimp in stomach contents suggests that Tribodus was a benthic feeder.
The genus Tribodus was described by Brito and Ferreira in 1989.
Unlike other hybodonts, the lower jaw of Tribodus was short, did not reach the snout, and articulated with the upper jaw exclusively at the hyoid arch.
Cartilage struts connected the upper and lower jaws of Tribodus, enhancing jaw strength.
It is hypothesized that Tribodus may have spawned in shallow-water vegetated areas.
Historically, Tribodus was classified in the family Acrodontidae based on columnar osteodentine in its teeth.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Tribodus as Hybodontidae.
Tribodus lived during the mid Cretaceous period, specifically from the Albian to Cenomanian stages.
Tribodus lived from the Aptian to the Cenomanian, between 119.57 and 93.9 million years ago.
Fossils of Tribodus have been found in northern South America, North Africa, and southern Europe.
Species of Tribodus inhabited shallow marine, fluvial, and deltaic environments.
Some researchers suggest placing Tribodus in the family Distobatidae because its tooth morphology resembles members of that family.
